definition: In computer graphics and computer vision, image-based modeling and rendering (IBMR) methods rely on a set of two-dimensional images of a scene to generate a three-dimensional model and then render some novel views of this scene.
details: The traditional approach of computer graphics has been used to create a geometric model in 3D and try to reproject it onto a two-dimensional image. Computer vision, conversely, is mostly focused on detecting, grouping, and extracting features (edges, faces, etc.) present in a given picture and then trying to interpret them as three-dimensional clues. Image-based modeling and rendering allows the use of multiple two-dimensional images in order to generate directly novel two-dimensional images, skipping the manual modeling stage.

explainer.lead: Image-based modeling and rendering (IBMR) uses a set of 2D images of a scene to generate a 3D model and render novel views. It matters because it produces new views directly from images rather than only from a hand-built geometric model.

tiers.eli5: Take several photos of a room from different spots, and the computer works out what the room looks like from places you never stood.
tiers.practitioner: Instead of building a 3D geometric model and reprojecting it, IBMR detects and groups features (edges, faces) across images and treats them as 3D clues. Pitfall: it depends on those extracted features being present and consistent across the input images.
tiers.paperLevel: Methods rely on multiple 2D images to generate a 3D model and novel 2D images, contrasting with geometry-first graphics and feature-extraction-first vision. Known limits follow from its dependence on the supplied image set.

explainer.example: Given several photographs of a scene, IBMR builds a 3D model and renders a two-dimensional view from a new viewpoint.
